episode.title: UPDATE: Gloria Steinem, Iran's economy and the Pentagon's testosterone pullback
episode.description:
Iran's beginning to buckle under the strain of recent U.S. economic pressure, according to Iranian sources. Feminist leader Gloria Steinem dies at the age of 92. Trump's pledge to get U.S. finances under control falls flat, creating a looming fiscal crunch. And Denmark deploys conscripts to Greenland for the first time in recent history.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: Iran's economy is showing signs of buckling under a US blockade and expanded sanctions. That's according to 3 senior Iranian sources. Oil exports have collapsed to just 260,000 barrels a day. That's down from 1.7 million a year ago. Iran's currency has lost more than half its value. Inflation is near 70%. And one source says Iran has only 2 months of gasoline supply left. The squeeze is cutting off Tehran's access to foreign currency and international financing networks that it's used to skirt previous sanctions for decades. The strain could bring Iran back to the negotiation table, but Iran officials warn they could respond with further military escalation.

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: Reuters has learned Tehran is warning Washington it would launch a large-scale attack if Israel moves on a contested ridge in southern Lebanon. According to two officials, Iranian Revolutionary Guard members, including senior officers, are there alongside Hezbollah fighters. Iran's warning, delivered via Oman last month, appears to have worked for now. One official says US pressure has led Israel to hold off on storming the site. But Lebanese security officials warn an Israeli operation there could still come within weeks.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: The Pentagon has temporarily pulled back new clinical guidance that would have mandated testosterone deficiency screening for all service members aged 30 and above. The guidance calling for blood tests for men and women to be screened for fatigue and menstrual irregularities was posted to the Defense Department's website on Wednesday, but just a day later, it was removed. A U.S. official told Reuters the draft is being rescinded to allow for updates and interim guidance remains in effect.

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: Medical experts are pushing back, saying there's little scientific evidence that universal screening for low testosterone would improve U.S. combat readiness. The FDA is set to convene its own expert panel on testosterone use later this month.

utterances.text: For more than 5 decades, she championed women's equality, reproductive rights, and social justice. Steinem helped found New York Magazine in the '60s and the National Women's Political Caucus in the early '70s. And in 1963, she published a groundbreaking exposé after spending 11 days as a Playboy Bunny, revealing the poor pay and sexist treatment women endured.

utterances.speaker: B

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: For the second time, a federal judge is blocking President Trump's attempt to limit birthright citizenship. The latest executive order signed in August came after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's original effort. Judge Deborah Boardman ruled the new order is almost certainly unconstitutional, saying the court has already decided the children covered by the case are citizens at birth. And sticking with the courts, Democrats are blocking a Republican push to permanently cap the number of Supreme Court justices at 9. Republicans had pushed the amendment to lock in the court's current 6-3 conservative majority ahead of the midterms. Democrats are proposing expanding the court to 13 justices.

President Donald Trump came back to the White House promising to get the US's finances in order, but the national debt crossed a milestone this summer, surging past $40 trillion. Budget experts say tax cuts, higher spending, rising borrowing costs, and the Iran conflict have pushed finances deeper into the red. The White House argues economic growth will ultimately ease the burden. But as reporter Jacob Bogage explains, with midterm elections coming and interest costs climbing, tough choices could be ahead.

At the end of the road, there's either going to be much higher taxes, much lower benefits, or a combination of both. And we've kind of reached the point where you can't get out of this debt spiral without causing pain.

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: And markets are watching that rising debt load closely, particularly in the bond market, where yields have been reflecting investor anxiety about the US fiscal trajectory. For more on what this all means, here's our Morning Bid host, Mike Dolan.
